newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-MALDINI IS ITALY'S SOCCER CAESAR.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-MALDINI IS ITALY'S SOCCER CAESAR.

text.p: When it comes to crowning a new soccer boss, Italy could hardly choose a more aptly-named coach than Cesare "Cesarone" (Big Caesar) Maldini.
The Germans had their all-conquering "Kaiser" Franz Beckenbauer and now Italy, who appointed Maldini as national soccer coach on Sunday, have their Caesar.
They also have a dynasty with the 64-year-old Cesare coaching a team captained by his son Paolo -- who himself became the father of a son Christian this year.
Both father and son have the records to command respect even in a nation where everyone wants to be coach -- or better still where everyone wants to tell the coach what to do.

While his predecessor Arrigo Sacchi started off as a travelling shoe salesman before working his way through the ranks as coach of lower league teams, Maldini knows what it is like to play in front of the big crowds.
Born the son of a navy official in the north-eastern Adriatic port of Trieste in 1932, Cesare began his career at local club Triestina, then a serie A team, in 1953.
His father Albino had been preparing him to be an orthodontist but Cesare had other ambitions.
Literally the blue-eyed boy, like his son, Cesare took the role of defender and soon caught the eye of AC Milan.
It was the beginning of a 12-year love affair with the northern club that ended with four league titles -- in 1955, 1957, 1959 and 1962 and the 1963 European Cup.
Maldini was the captain in the final against Portugal's Benfica at Wembley, lifting the cup after a 2-1 win.
His last serie A match came on May 28, 1967 when he had moved to Torino. He had played 14 times for Italy, wearing the captain's armband six times from 1962 to 1963.
He was sent off only twice in his career -- once in the league against Roma and once in the Intercontinental Cup final against Santos of Brazil of 1963 which Santos won.
The glory did not stop on hanging up his boots.
He coached the junior team at Milan, then took Parma from the third division to the second in 1979.
He had poor spells at Foggia and Terni before becoming deputy to national coach Enzo Bearzot in 1980, helping bring the World Cup to Italy for the third time in 1982.
When under-21 coach Azeglio Vicini was appointed Italy coach in 1986, Maldini took his role with the youngsters.
His success and fame increased steadily.

As under-21 coach, Maldini won the European under-21 championship three times and, more importantly, picked teams that kept on entertaining at a time when the senior squad was going through a difficult phase under Sacchi.
The only rough patch came last summer when Italy was looking to Maldini to bring home Olympic gold from Atlanta but the under-21 team disappointed and returned empty-handed.
An old-school coach with modern views, Maldini has been labelled a man whose expertise lies more in the selection of players than in enforcing complicated tactics.
If picked by Maldini, the odds are that the player will appear in the same position he plays in successfully at club level rather than being forced to take on new roles.
In February Italians will find out just how the team plays under his guidance when he steps back down memory lane to Wembley for a key World Cup qualifier against England.
"If the senior team can repeat the success of the magical under-21 team, he will find he suddenly has several million more friends," commented the daily Gazzetta dello Sport.
There will be no cup to raise there this time. Just the hopes of a nation hoping for great times ahead.
